message.content:
The last common ancestor of a lion (Panthera leo) and a zebra (Equus quagga) is a **placental mammal that lived in the late Paleocene (roughly 65–70 million years ago)**.  

- **Lion** belongs to the family **Felidae** in the order **Carnivora**.  
- **Zebra** belongs to the family **Equidae** in the order **Perissodactyla** (odd‑toed ungulates).  

The two lineages diverged after the split between the clades that contain Carnivora and Perissodactyla. Their last common ancestor would have been a small, insectivorous or omnivorous mammal that gave rise to the diverse groups of placental mammals we see today.

The common ancestor would be a mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. That is the ancestor of the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the clade of the group called "Perissodactyla + Carnivora" which is part of the clade "Perissodactyla + Artiodactyla"? Actually, the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla is the ancestor of the clade "Perissodactyla + Carnivora" which is part of the clade "Perissodactyla + Artiodactyla" (even-toed ungulates). But the last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older. So the answer: The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is a mammalian ancestor that lived around 70-80 million years ago, likely a small, insectivorous mammal. But we can say: The last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae is a mammal that lived in the Paleocene, around 65-70 million years ago. So answer accordingly.
